messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Minh's Vigilance

Minh was eighty-two when he came to the clinic, though the weariness in his face suggested someone older. He had spent the better part of three decades as a data scientist, building predictive models for financial institutions, work that had suited his methodical mind. But it was what had happened forty-seven years ago—during his time as a relief worker in Cambodia in 1977—that had quietly reshaped everything about how he moved through the world.

The assignment had seemed purposeful then. Minh, younger and idealistic, had crossed into the country to deliver medical supplies and document conditions in a rural province. What he encountered was systematic cruelty on a scale that fractured something fundamental in his understanding of human nature. He had watched soldiers execute civilians for minor infractions—a man beaten to death for speaking out of turn, a woman shot for attempting to shield her child. The randomness of it haunted him still: the same transgression might be ignored one day and trigger lethal violence the next. What remained most visceral was the feeling of absolute powerlessness, the knowledge that no amount of reasoning or compliance could predict or prevent what would happen next. He had eventually fled, carrying those images like shrapnel embedded too deep to remove.

For decades, Minh had managed. He built a life, married a Vietnamese woman named Linh, raised two daughters. When Linh died five years ago, he had grieved but continued. The memories stayed buried, accessed only in dreams. But something shifted recently—a news report about political violence in Southeast Asia had caught him unprepared one evening, and since then, the careful architecture of his life had begun to crack.

Now, when Minh saw footage of civil unrest or read about authoritarian crackdowns, the memories erupted unbidden. A report about police brutality triggered the full cascade: the film began to play, frame by frame, and he felt himself back in that province, the heat oppressive, the sounds of violence immediate and real. When the memory came, it didn't feel like remembering something distant—it felt like the event was happening to him right now, as vivid and present as breath. The reliving was so complete that he would sometimes check his hands, expecting to find blood. These episodes terrified him, and he had come to believe that his mind was fracturing, that his reactions since the trauma meant he was going crazy. This fear fed a new conviction: that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that cruelty lurked beneath every interaction, waiting to emerge.

The triggers had multiplied and woven themselves into his daily existence. When people behaved badly—a neighbor's curt remark, a rude cashier—Minh's nervous system responded as though witnessing the same moral violation he had seen in Cambodia: the sudden, arbitrary cruelty that revealed human nature as fundamentally corrupt. Any situation where he felt trapped without options—a doctor's appointment where he couldn't leave early, a family dinner where he felt obligated to attend—activated the old sense of entrapment, and the memories would surge forward. Even waking from nightmares left him disoriented, the boundary between sleep and waking permeable, the threat feeling as real as when he had first lived it.

To manage the memories and the terror they brought, Minh had developed an elaborate system of avoidance and control. He stopped watching news entirely, turning off the television or leaving the room when reports of violence appeared. This had cost him—his daughters had noticed his withdrawal, had asked why he never engaged with current events anymore, had stopped inviting him to family gatherings where he might encounter unexpected triggers. At work, before any meeting or interaction, he rehearsed what he would say, running through conversations repeatedly in his mind to anticipate how others might respond unpredictably or behave badly. His colleagues had begun to comment that he seemed rigid, over-prepared, anxious in ways that seemed disproportionate to a simple team meeting. Most exhausting was his constant scanning of his environment. At the grocery store, on walks through his neighborhood, even in his own home, Minh's attention was perpetually divided. His body remained tense, coiled, ready to react to danger that he was certain was present but invisible. He found himself tracking exits, noting who stood near him, assessing threats in the casual movements of strangers.

The memory rehearsals, meant to contain the trauma, had paradoxically strengthened it. Each time he mentally prepared for a conversation, he would find himself slipping back into the memories—the anticipatory anxiety would trigger the film to play again, and the cycle would tighten. His hypervigilance, his constant threat-scanning, kept his nervous system in a state of perpetual alarm that made the memories feel more urgent, more real. His body was always on alert, muscles tight, ready to react. When he did manage to relax, even briefly, irritability would surface—sudden anger at small things, a sharpness in his voice that surprised even him. He had snapped at his eldest daughter during a recent phone call, had felt the rage building in his chest and been terrified by his own capacity for it, which only reinforced his fear that he was losing control, that his mind was deteriorating.

Minh came to the clinic because his daughter had insisted, and because he had begun to wonder if the constant vigilance, the endless mental rehearsals, the avoidance that had narrowed his world to a small, safe perimeter, were worth the cost of living this way. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the possibility that they would never fade, that he would spend his remaining years trapped in a present moment that never ended.
